title: Neighbours That Add Up to a Square

concept.title: Only extend the arrangement with numbers that make a perfect square with the last one
body: Arrange the given numbers in a row so that **each two neighbours add up to a perfect square** (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, ...). Count the different arrangements; if the array has equal numbers, two arrangements that look the same count once. This is a permutation search with a rule between **neighbouring** choices, and with duplicates to handle.

Sort the numbers, then build the arrangement from left to right. A number can be placed after the last one only if their sum is a perfect square. To handle the equal numbers, use the usual rule: **if a number equals the previous number in the sorted list and that previous number has not been used (in this branch), skip it**; otherwise the same arrangement would be produced for both copies.

The perfect-square test uses the integer square root: `r = isqrt(x)` and `r * r == x`. Since the rule prunes at **every step** (only a few numbers fit after a given one), the search is much smaller than the `12!` of all orders. The count can be zero.

statement: You are given `n` non-negative integers; some may be equal. Count the different arrangements of the numbers in a row such that the sum of every two neighbouring numbers is a perfect square (0 is a perfect square). Two arrangements are the same if they have the same numbers in every position.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` integers.
outputFormat: Print the number of arrangements (it can be 0).
hints: Sort the numbers and build the row from left to right.
A number may follow the last one only if their sum is a perfect square; use an integer square root to test this.
Skip a number equal to the previous one when the previous copy is still unused.

explanation: After sorting, the row is built from left to right. A number is tried only if it is unused, if it is not a repeated copy whose earlier copy is unused, and if its sum with the last number is a perfect square. A complete row counts one.
solution.complexity: Time proportional to the number of partial arrangements (small thanks to the square rule), space O(n).
